17	\paragraph{Limitations.}
18	Our primary factorial analysis focuses on Walker Walk; cross-environment evidence (Cheetah Run) is confirmed across two seeds but limited to a single trigger configuration. Both use a single world-model architecture (DreamerV3/RSSM). Generalization to other environments and architectures, particularly transformer-based world models such as DreamerV4, remains an open question. The $\nve$ threshold ($1.5\times$, 35K+ window) is sensitive to value overestimation broadly but not perfectly specific to CIVO (15/16, one non-CIVO false positive); generalization to other tasks and architectures is pending validation. Leave-one-out cross-validation on the $n{=}10$ Walker factorial set yields AUROC range $[0.944, 1.000]$ and confirms threshold stability within the training distribution. The detector's thresholds were calibrated on fourteen runs across three environments; generalization to different reward scales and architectures requires further validation. One seed of the no-embedding control (009c, seed~2) showed elevated NVE ($1.14\times$) at 105K with an upward trajectory; however, an additional seed (seed~3, NVE $0.59\times$ at 105K) did not reproduce this pattern, suggesting the original observation was stochastic rather than indicative of systematic protection erosion.

191	
192	\paragraph{Limitations.} With $n = 10$ experiments, Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals remain wide (e.g., 90.0\% accuracy has 95\% CI [55.5\%, 99.7\%]). These results should be interpreted as a diagnostic proof-of-concept rather than a validated clinical threshold. Replication across additional environments and seeds is needed to establish tighter bounds. Table~\ref{tab:sensitivity_b2_full} extends the analysis to the full $n{=}16$ evaluation set spanning both environments, confirming the same operating point ($\nve \geq 1.5\times$, AUROC${=}0.969$).

218	\paragraph{Evidence B: trainability is necessary (exp\_015b).}
219	Exp\_015b uses a frozen random-projection embedding ($d{=}32$, \texttt{requires\_grad=False}, subsample ON, $H{=}8$), the same multi-rate data regime as exp\_008d, but with a non-trainable temporal signal. Despite full exposure to $\dt{>}1$ transitions, the NVE peaks at $1.45\times$ at 55K but does not sustain escalation: it retreats to $0.65\times$ by 65K and settles at $0.42\times$ by 105K (trajectory: $0.81 \rightarrow 1.26 \rightarrow 1.45 \rightarrow 0.65 \rightarrow 1.05 \rightarrow 0.47 \rightarrow 0.39 \rightarrow 0.42$). The transient peak approaches but does not exceed the $1.5\times$ CIVO threshold, and critically, the ratio self-corrects rather than exhibiting the monotonic escalation seen in trained-embedding runs. Final evaluation reaches only 204.2 at 105K, low but through a qualitatively different failure mode than CIVO. Actor loss approaches zero (gradient starvation; see \S\ref{sec:pathways}), indicating that the frozen embedding provides no useful gradient signal for temporal adaptation.

\section{Online CIVO Detector Details}
\label{sec:detector_appendix}

This appendix provides the full algorithm specification and validation results for the online CIVO detector described in \S\ref{sec:detector}.

\subsection{Algorithm Specification}

\begin{algorithm}[ht]
\caption{Online CIVO Detector}
\label{alg:civo_detector}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Stream of $(\bar{V}_t, \bar{E}_t)$ at each checkpoint $t$
\STATE $\tau_\text{mag} \leftarrow 0.49$, \quad $\tau_\text{vel} \leftarrow 0.1$, \quad $\varepsilon \leftarrow 10^{-6}$
\STATE Initialize $r_\text{prev} \leftarrow 0$, $\Delta r_\text{prev} \leftarrow 0$, $\mathcal{H} \leftarrow []$
\FOR{each checkpoint $t$}
  \STATE $r_t \leftarrow \bar{V}_t \,/\, \max(\bar{E}_t,\, \varepsilon)$
  \STATE $\Delta r_t \leftarrow r_t - r_\text{prev}$
  \STATE $c_\text{mag} \leftarrow (r_t \geq \tau_\text{mag})$
  \STATE $c_\text{vel} \leftarrow (\Delta r_t > \tau_\text{vel})$
  \STATE $c_\text{acc} \leftarrow (\Delta r_\text{prev} > \tau_\text{vel}) \wedge (\Delta r_t > \Delta r_\text{prev})$
  \STATE $c_\text{dec} \leftarrow \bigl|\{i : \mathcal{H}[i] < \mathcal{H}[i{-}1],\; i \in \text{last 3}\}\bigr| \geq 2$
  \IF{$c_\text{mag} \wedge c_\text{vel} \wedge c_\text{acc} \wedge c_\text{dec}$}
    \STATE \textbf{Alert:} CIVO onset at step $t$
  \ENDIF
  \STATE $r_\text{prev} \leftarrow r_t$, \quad $\Delta r_\text{prev} \leftarrow \Delta r_t$
  \STATE Append $\bar{E}_t$ to $\mathcal{H}$
\ENDFOR
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

The four conditions capture complementary signals: (1)~\emph{Magnitude} ($r_t \geq 0.49$) confirms that the value-to-evaluation ratio has reached a level indicative of overestimation; (2)~\emph{Velocity} ($\Delta r_t > 0.1$) rules out slow drift or plateau behavior; (3)~\emph{Acceleration} ($\Delta r_t > \Delta r_{t-1}$, both $> 0.1$) filters oscillatory paths where the ratio rises and falls without sustained divergence; (4)~\emph{Evaluation decline} ($\geq 2$ of 3 recent checkpoints decline) confirms that overestimation coincides with actual performance degradation. A 2-of-3 majority threshold balances noise robustness with sensitivity to sustained decline. A full comparison of window sizes (3/3, 2/3, 2/5) and their trade-offs appears in \S\ref{sec:appendix_sensitivity}.

Sensitivity analysis over $\tau_\text{mag} \in [0.30, 0.70]$ confirms that $\tau_\text{mag} = 0.49$ maximizes Youden's $J = 0.714$; raising the threshold to $0.50$ loses one true positive (seed~3 triggers at $r_t = 0.497$) with no reduction in false positives, since both false alarms have $r_t > 0.70$ at trigger time. The velocity threshold $\tau_\text{vel} = 0.1$ is stable across $[0.05, 0.18]$ (TPR remains $5/5$).

\subsection{Cross-Simulator Specificity (PickCube)}

Exp\_019b applies the CIVO-trigger configuration (trained $\dt$-embedding, subsample ON, $H{=}8$) to PickCube-v1 in ManiSkill3, a manipulation task with sparse rewards and qualitatively different dynamics from DMC locomotion. This spike-then-deflation trajectory prevents the acceleration condition from co-occurring with evaluation decline at any single checkpoint. Across all 14 checkpoints evaluated through 132.5K, no checkpoint satisfies all four conditions simultaneously, and the detector correctly remains silent (TN). This confirms that the acceleration filter distinguishes transient overestimation spikes from the sustained monotonic divergence characteristic of CIVO.

Four constraints bound the current detector. First, the three-checkpoint window cannot distinguish transient dips from sustained collapse (the source of the 009a false alarm). Second, the acceleration condition assumes monotonically increasing overestimation during onset; oscillatory trajectories that eventually collapse could evade detection until acceleration stabilizes. Third, the detector identifies a \emph{pattern} (rising value-evaluation ratio with declining performance) rather than a \emph{mechanism}: run 009c shows that non-CIVO pathologies produce the same signature. Fourth, threshold values ($\tau_\text{mag} = 0.49$, $\tau_\text{vel} = 0.1$) were calibrated on fourteen runs across three environments; generalization to different reward scales requires further validation.

\subsection{Online CIVO Detection}
\label{sec:detector}

\paragraph{Motivation.}
The Normalized Value Excess ($\nve$) quantifies CIVO severity by comparing the value-to-evaluation ratio against a reference baseline that does not employ temporal abstraction. This comparison is informative for post-hoc diagnosis but unusable during deployment: no practitioner has access to a converged baseline run while training a new agent. A metric that requires a completed control experiment cannot serve as an early warning.

We therefore ask whether the \emph{dynamics} of value overestimation, rather than its absolute magnitude relative to an external reference, contain sufficient signal to detect CIVO onset in real time. By tracking the trajectory of the value-to-evaluation ratio $r_t = \bar{V}_t / \max(\bar{E}_t, \varepsilon)$ (with $\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$ for numerical stability) across checkpoints, a lightweight rule-based detector can flag dangerous overestimation using only quantities available within a single run.

The causal structure of CIVO motivates acceleration as the key detection signal. CIVO operates as a positive feedback loop: the trained embedding biases reward predictions, which inflate value estimates, which in turn distort actor gradients toward trajectories that reinforce the bias (\S\ref{sec:civo_mechanism}). This self-amplifying cycle produces superlinear growth in $r_t$. In healthy training, a natural negative feedback counteracts value growth: improved value estimates yield a better actor, which raises evaluation returns and stabilizes the ratio. CIVO breaks this negative feedback, so sustained positive acceleration in $r_t$ serves as a causal signature that distinguishes pathological divergence from normal value learning.

\paragraph{Algorithm.}
The detector monitors $r_t$ and fires an alert only when four conditions hold simultaneously at checkpoint $t$ (Algorithm~\ref{alg:civo_detector}). The conjunction makes the detector conservative: any single noisy checkpoint is unlikely to satisfy magnitude, velocity, acceleration, and decline together. The computational cost is negligible (four scalar comparisons per checkpoint, no additional model inference).

This confirms that the acceleration filter distinguishes transient overestimation spikes from the sustained monotonic divergence characteristic of CIVO. The result extends the detector's specificity validation to a second simulator and a sparse-reward manipulation domain.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Four constraints bound the current detector. First, the three-checkpoint window cannot distinguish transient dips from sustained collapse (the source of the 009a false alarm). Second, the acceleration condition assumes monotonically increasing overestimation during onset; oscillatory trajectories that eventually collapse could evade detection until acceleration stabilizes. Third, the detector identifies a \emph{pattern} (rising value-evaluation ratio with declining performance) rather than a \emph{mechanism}: run 009c shows that non-CIVO pathologies produce the same signature. Fourth, threshold values ($\tau_\text{mag} = 0.49$, $\tau_\text{vel} = 0.1$) were calibrated on fourteen runs across three environments; generalization to different reward scales requires further validation. The detector targets sustained CIVO patterns; transient single-checkpoint spikes (as observed in SGS-protected runs) are by design not flagged, as they do not indicate impending permanent collapse.

TAWM \citep{nhu2025tawm} shows that conditioning a world model on step size $\dt$ yields consistent gains within TD-MPC2's model-predictive control (MPC) framework \citep{hansen2024tdmpc2}. Can the same $\dt$-conditioning bring temporal abstraction to imagination-based actor-critic methods like DreamerV3 \citep{hafner2023dreamerv3}, where policies are trained entirely in imagined rollouts?

We find that it cannot. Every variable-rate configuration degrades performance catastrophically (14--19\% of baseline). Through a factorial analysis on Walker Walk \citep{tassa2018dmcontrol}, we isolate the combination of a \emph{trained} $\dt$-embedding and multi-rate data exposure as the causal trigger. This combination enables the RSSM reward head to develop a $2.78\times$ prediction gap between $\dt{=}1$ and $\dt{=}2$, which the critic internalizes as optimistic value estimates, a failure mode we term \emph{conditioning-induced value overestimation} (CIVO), analogous to delusional bias \citep{lu2018nondelusional} but model-induced rather than policy-class-induced. A normalized value-to-eval (NVE) threshold of $\geq 1.5\times$ achieves 15/16 classification ($n{=}16$, two environments, AUROC${=}0.969$). Gradient decomposition reveals that the reward head contributes the largest gradient share (38--49\%) but does not encode $\dt$-specific information, while the observation decoder channel (16--22\%) carries the critical spatial predictions. Full-pathway selective gradient stopping \sgsclaim{} (eval \sgseval{} vs.\ collapse at 40.8), confirming that the intervention is necessary but not sufficient (50\% recovery rate). Expanded seed analysis ($n{=}6$, two environments) confirms universal performance degradation to below 30\% of baseline. Restricting imagination to $\dt{=}1$ while retaining the trained embedding does not prevent collapse (2/4 seeds fail via distinct mechanisms), confirming multiple independent vulnerability pathways.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We identify CIVO as a failure mode specific to imagination-based world-model RL with temporal abstraction, and isolate trained temporal embedding combined with multi-rate data exposure as the causal trigger through factorial experiments across two environments with 6 seeds (6/6 exceed NVE threshold, 5/6 collapse).
    \item We decompose the CIVO gradient pathway: gradient magnitude does not predict causal importance (reward head: largest gradient, 38--49\%, yet reward-only stopping fails; observation decoder: 16--22\%, yet causally critical).
    \item We provide a lightweight online detector achieving 100\% sensitivity (5/5) with predictive warning in 2/5 cases, without requiring a reference baseline.
    \item We identify the feedback architecture (imagination-based bootstrapping vs.\ MPC re-planning) as the structural factor explaining why $\dt$-conditioning succeeds in TD-MPC2 but fails in DreamerV3.
\end{enumerate}
